blocks.text: In 1982 a group of young drug users in California suddenly became rigid, slow and unable to move, as if they had advanced Parkinson disease. The cause was a contaminant, MPTP, in a synthetic opioid. It killed one small group of dopamine-producing neurones in the midbrain. A single transmitter system, damaged, produced a whole movement disorder.

blocks.markdown:
Neurones are classified by the principal transmitter they release. A **transmitter system** is the set of neurones that make a given transmitter, their pathways, the receptors that respond to it, and the mechanisms that synthesise and remove it. The clinically most important systems for this course are the **cholinergic**, **dopaminergic** and **GABAergic** systems, alongside glutamate (the main excitatory transmitter), serotonin and noradrenaline.

- **Cholinergic**: principal transmitter **acetylcholine (ACh)**, made from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase and broken down in the cleft by acetylcholinesterase. ACh is the transmitter of all lower motor neurones at the neuromuscular junction, all autonomic preganglionic neurones, parasympathetic postganglionic neurones, and basal forebrain neurones projecting to cortex.
- **Dopaminergic**: principal transmitter **dopamine**, made from tyrosine via L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme; DOPA decarboxylase makes dopamine). Pathways include the nigrostriatal (movement), mesolimbic (reward) and mesocortical pathways.
- **GABAergic**: principal transmitter **gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)**, the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain, made from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase. Its receptors include the ionotropic GABA-A (Cl- channel) and the metabotropic GABA-B.

rows: Neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia, parasympathetic targets, basal forebrain
Cortical and striatal interneurones, cerebellar Purkinje cells
Most excitatory neurones of cortex and thalamus

blocks.title: Nigrostriatal pathway
blocks.text: The nigrostriatal pathway is formed by dopaminergic neurones whose cell bodies lie in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and whose axons project to the striatum (caudate and putamen). Dopamine released there modulates striatal output and facilitates initiation and scaling of voluntary movement.

blocks.markdown:
In **Parkinson disease** the SNc neurones degenerate, so striatal dopamine falls markedly. Clinical features follow from loss of dopamine's facilitation of movement: **bradykinesia** (slowness and reduced amplitude of movement), **rigidity** (increased tone, often cogwheel), a **rest tremor** and later postural instability. Symptoms usually emerge only after a large fraction of nigral neurones has been lost, because the surviving neurones compensate.

Because dopamine itself does not cross the blood-brain barrier, replacement therapy uses its precursor **levodopa (L-DOPA)**, which does and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase in surviving terminals. This is a pharmacology teaching example, not treatment advice.

blocks.title: Excess acetylcholine from enzyme inhibition
blocks.prompt: A farm worker is exposed to an organophosphate pesticide, which irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Predict the cholinergic effects.

steps.text: Acetylcholinesterase normally hydrolyses ACh in the synaptic cleft. With it inhibited, ACh persists and keeps stimulating its receptors.
Muscarinic receptors on parasympathetic targets are overstimulated: salivation, lacrimation, bronchial secretion and constriction, bradycardia, miosis, increased gut motility.
Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction are overstimulated: fasciculations at first, then weakness from persistent depolarisation.

blocks.answer: A syndrome of excess cholinergic activity: wet secretions, small pupils, slow heart rate, fasciculations and weakness. This follows from ACh being the principal transmitter at both muscarinic and nicotinic synapses.

blocks.markdown: **Drugs that alter reuptake.** After release, many transmitters are removed from the cleft by **transporters** on the presynaptic terminal (or glia). Dopamine is taken up by the dopamine transporter (DAT), serotonin by SERT and noradrenaline by NET. A **reuptake inhibitor** blocks the transporter, so for each release event the transmitter stays in the cleft longer and at higher concentration, increasing and prolonging receptor activation. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block SERT; cocaine blocks DAT and NET and SERT. Reuptake blockers do not increase release; they slow removal.

blocks.title: Reasoning about a reuptake inhibitor
blocks.prompt: A drug blocks the serotonin transporter. Explain how this changes synaptic signalling at a serotonergic synapse, and why the effect may take time to be felt clinically.

steps.text: Baseline: serotonin is released, binds postsynaptic and autoreceptors, and is cleared mainly by SERT.
With SERT blocked, removal is slower, so synaptic serotonin concentration and duration rise and postsynaptic receptors are activated more.
The system adapts: presynaptic autoreceptors and receptor expression change over days to weeks, which is one proposed reason for the delay in clinical benefit.

blocks.answer: Synaptic serotonin signalling is amplified and prolonged because clearance is reduced. The initial biochemical effect is rapid, but adaptive changes mean clinical effects develop over weeks.

items: Glutamate excites and GABA inhibits: most neural computation is a balance between the two.
ACh acts on nicotinic (fast, ionotropic) and muscarinic (slower, metabotropic) receptors.
Dopamine receptors are all G-protein-coupled; there is no ionotropic dopamine receptor.
A drug can alter signalling by changing synthesis, release, receptor binding, breakdown or reuptake.

blocks.title: Do not mix up the systems
blocks.text: In Parkinson disease the loss is of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway, not a loss of acetylcholine or GABA. Do not confuse reuptake inhibition (slows removal, no extra release) with a releasing agent or with enzyme inhibition (which blocks breakdown).

points: The principal transmitters are acetylcholine (cholinergic), dopamine (dopaminergic) and GABA (GABAergic, the main inhibitory transmitter).
The nigrostriatal pathway runs from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum; its degeneration causes bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.
Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine, unlike dopamine itself.
Reuptake inhibitors block transporters so transmitter remains longer in the cleft, amplifying signalling without increasing release.

questions.stem: Which is the principal transmitter released by a lower motor neurone at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?

distractorRationale.a: Dopamine is the transmitter of nigrostriatal and mesolimbic pathways.
distractorRationale.b: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain.
distractorRationale.c: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the CNS, not at the neuromuscular junction.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: motor neurones are cholinergic and act on nicotinic receptors on muscle.

questions.explanation: Lower motor neurones are cholinergic: they release acetylcholine, which binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate. This is the classical example of a cholinergic synapse.

questions.stem: Which transmitter is the principal inhibitory transmitter of the adult brain?

distractorRationale.a: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter.
distractorRationale.b: Acetylcholine is excitatory at nicotinic receptors and has mixed effects at muscarinic ones.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: GABA acts at GABA-A Cl- channels and GABA-B receptors to inhibit neurones.
distractorRationale.d: Noradrenaline is a modulatory transmitter, not the principal inhibitor.

questions.explanation: GABA is made from glutamate and opens Cl- channels (GABA-A) or activates G-protein-coupled receptors (GABA-B) that hyperpolarise neurones. GABAergic interneurones balance glutamatergic excitation.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of a transmitter at its ionotropic receptor and produce sedation and anticonvulsant effects. Which transmitter system do they potentiate? (Pharmacology teaching example.)

distractorRationale.b: Cholinergic enhancement would not typically sedate.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: benzodiazepines enhance GABA action at GABA-A receptors, increasing inhibition.

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines bind a site on the GABA-A receptor and increase the effect of GABA on the Cl- channel. More inhibition lowers neuronal excitability, giving sedative and anticonvulsant effects.

questions.stem: In Parkinson disease, which neurones degenerate to produce the characteristic motor features?

options.text: Dopaminergic neurones of the substantia nigra pars compacta projecting to the striatum
Cholinergic neurones of the neuromuscular junction
GABAergic Purkinje cells of the cerebellum
Serotonergic neurones of the raphe nuclei

questions.correctOptionText: Dopaminergic neurones of the substantia nigra pars compacta projecting to the striatum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of nigrostriatal dopamine is the hallmark.
distractorRationale.b: Neuromuscular junction failure causes weakness, as in myasthenia, not parkinsonism.
distractorRationale.d: Raphe serotonergic neurones are not the primary lesion in Parkinson disease.

questions.explanation: The nigrostriatal pathway arises from dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Their degeneration leaves the striatum deficient in dopamine, producing bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.

questions.stem: Why is levodopa, rather than dopamine itself, used in dopamine replacement for parkinsonism? (Teaching example, not treatment advice.)

options.text: Dopamine is not synthesised in the body
Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain
Dopamine acts only on ionotropic receptors that levodopa activates directly

questions.correctOptionText: Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain

distractorRationale.a: Levodopa is a precursor, not a reuptake blocker.
distractorRationale.b: Dopamine is synthesised from tyrosine via L-DOPA.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: dopamine itself does not enter the brain adequately but levodopa does.
distractorRationale.d: Dopamine receptors are metabotropic and levodopa has no direct receptor action.

questions.explanation: Peripherally given dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, whereas its precursor levodopa can. In the brain DOPA decarboxylase converts it to dopamine in remaining dopaminergic terminals.

questions.stem: True or false: the rigidity and bradykinesia of Parkinson disease result from excess dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway.
questions.explanation: Parkinsonian features result from a deficiency of dopamine because nigrostriatal neurones degenerate. Excess dopaminergic activity is associated with hyperkinetic and psychotic effects, not with bradykinesia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has slowness of movement, a pill-rolling rest tremor and increased limb tone. Explain how depletion of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway accounts for these features, and the rationale for giving a dopamine precursor.
markingGuide: Degeneration of dopaminergic SNc neurones that project to the striatum
Reduced striatal dopamine impairs facilitation of voluntary movement, causing bradykinesia
Rigidity and rest tremor are also consequences of nigrostriatal dopamine deficiency
Dopamine does not cross the blood-brain barrier; levodopa does
Levodopa is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase in surviving terminals
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra pars compacta supplies the striatum with dopamine, which facilitates movement initiation. When these neurones are lost, slowness, rigidity and rest tremor appear; levodopa replenishes dopamine because it crosses the blood-brain barrier.

questions.stem: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor increases serotonin signalling mainly by which mechanism?

options.text: Increasing vesicle fusion in the presynaptic terminal
Blocking the serotonin transporter so serotonin remains longer in the cleft

questions.correctOptionText: Blocking the serotonin transporter so serotonin remains longer in the cleft

distractorRationale.a: That describes an agonist, not a reuptake inhibitor.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: SERT blockade slows removal and prolongs and increases receptor activation.

questions.explanation: SSRIs bind SERT and prevent reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic terminal. The same amount released therefore stays in the cleft longer, prolonging its action on receptors.

questions.stem: Assume released transmitter is cleared from the cleft by first-order (exponential) removal, so the concentration remaining is C0 x exp(-t/tau). With a reuptake inhibitor present, tau rises to 5.0 ms. What percentage of the initial transmitter remains 5.0 ms after release?
questions.explanation: Fraction remaining = exp(-t/tau) = exp(-5.0/5.0) = exp(-1) = 0.368, so 36.8%. If tau had been 2.0 ms (no blocker), the fraction would be exp(-2.5) = 8.2%, so blocking reuptake leaves several times more transmitter available to bind receptors.

questions.stem: Cocaine blocks the dopamine transporter. Explain how this alters dopaminergic signalling in the synapse, and state one thing it does not do compared with a drug that increases dopamine release.
markingGuide: Dopamine is normally removed from the cleft by reuptake via DAT
Blocking DAT prolongs dopamine's time in the cleft and raises its concentration
Receptor activation is therefore increased and prolonged, strongest where dopamine is being released
A reuptake blocker does not itself increase vesicular release of dopamine
questions.explanation: Blocking DAT slows clearance, so each release event produces a larger and longer postsynaptic effect. Unlike a releasing agent, the blocker depends on existing neuronal release and does not increase how much is released.
